title: Prajnaparadha: The Crime Against Wisdom
description: Prajnaparadha: knowingly acting against what you already know your body needs. Overriding the natural sleep window is not insomnia, it is a choice.
content:
Charaka described something he called prajnaparadha, which translates roughly as "the crime against wisdom" as one of the three root causes of disease. His definition: knowingly acting in opposition to what you already know to be good for you. Overriding the body's signals with the mind's agenda.

The body sends a clear signal when it's ready for sleep. Drowsiness in the early evening. Heavy eyelids. A cooling sensation. The body temperature dropping. Melatonin rising. This window what chronobiologists now call the circadian sleep phase is specific to each person, but it is real and it is consistent. If you work with it, you fall asleep easily and the sleep is deep. If you override it with a screen, a second wind, one more hour of work, or a late meal you close the window. The next one doesn't open for ninety minutes to two hours. You lie awake, mind running, sleep won't come. That's not insomnia. That's prajnaparadha.

Charaka's framework was clinical. When a patient presented with sleep difficulties, his diagnostic process included: are you eating at irregular times? Are you working in the evening hours when the body wants to wind down? Are you suppressing natural sleep cues when they arise? Are you chronically anxious, which in Ayurvedic terms means vata is dysregulated, and the mind is running at night because the nervous system never received a clear signal to stop?

The stress-sleep relationship is not simply that stress causes arousal which prevents sleep. The mechanism is more specific. Chronic stress elevates cortisol. Cortisol follows a natural diurnal curve, high in the morning, and low at night that tells the body when to be alert and when to rest. Chronic stress disrupts this curve, often elevating cortisol in the evening when it should be dropping. Evening cortisol is incompatible with the melatonin rise that initiates sleep. The system fights itself.

The practices Charaka would prescribe for this:

First: a consistent sleep window, same time every night, even on weekends. This is the single most evidence supported behavioral intervention for sleep. The circadian system is set by consistency. Variability degrades it. You cannot sleep in on weekends and have good weeknight sleep. The system doesn't bank.

Second: an evening boundary for stimulation. Not a guideline, a physical boundary. Work ends at a specific time. Screens reduce or stop ninety minutes before sleep. The nervous system needs inputs to taper, not cut off abruptly. The gradual reduction of light, activity, and novelty allows cortisol to drop naturally.

Third: something warm before bed. Warm milk, herbal tea, haldi doodh. Warm liquid raises peripheral temperature (hands, feet) which accelerates core temperature drop - the physiological prerequisite for sleep onset. Charaka prescribed this as part of Dinacharya. The mechanism is why it works.

Fourth: stop reviewing tomorrow before sleep. The planning, worrying, and problem-solving the mind does in the last hour before sleep is prajnaparadha in real time you are telling a system that needs to downregulate to keep running. A physical notebook on the bedside table to offload the active loops is more effective than you'd expect. The mind will stop generating content it's already stored somewhere.

Stress is the circumstance. The practice is the intervention. You cannot remove most of the stressors. You can stop overriding what you already know your body needs.
